paras: The Rhea County quadruple lynching was the reported killing by a mob, in May 1888, of four Black men held in the jail at Washington, the seat of Rhea County, Tennessee, after they were accused of assaulting a white woman and her daughter. A Chattanooga dispatch named the four as James Strickland, Nick Webster, Jerry Long and Sam Sibner and predicted that a mob would lynch them; a day later, a Spring City special reported that it had. Every report of the lynching was second-hand, and the coverage contains no local confirmation, inquest or arrests.

According to a Chattanooga dispatch dated May 18, Mrs. Rice, a white widow with three children, was looking for work near the Kenrick ore mines in northern Rhea County and stopped for the night in a vacant house. The dispatch said four men it called "negroes" broke in about 10 o'clock, assaulted her at the point of a revolver, injured her twelve-year-old daughter, and attacked her again at 4 o'clock the next morning. Later reports described the accused as "negro laborers on a new railroad" and gave the woman's name as Mrs. Jane Whitney.

The men fled, the dispatch continued, but officers soon captured them and lodged them in the jail at Washington on the afternoon of May 18, and Mrs. Rice identified each of them. It closed with a special's word that a mob would lynch them that night or the next, and that the whole county was "up in arms." A Chattanooga report printed in the Atlanta Constitution on May 22 told the story differently: two of the men assaulted the widow while the other two tried to assault her daughter, who escaped and raised an alarm, and a "large posse" captured three of the four. Travelers from the remote district told Chattanooga that a quadruple lynching was sure within days if the arrested men proved guilty.

On May 19, however, a Spring City special sent by wire from Chicago said it was "reported" that four Black laborers had been lynched near Worthington. A fuller Spring City special, printed in late May, said word had reached the town from Washington that the four men "were taken from jail by an infuriated mob and lynched." A news digest in the Olneyville Times placed the lynching on the night of Friday, the day of the arrests. None of these reports described how the men were killed or named anyone in the mob.

The Spring City special added that "great excitement" prevailed among Black residents, "some of whom swear vengeance." No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members or of any official response appears in the coverage, and no later account confirms or denies the deaths.

The first reports, from Chattanooga, ran under headlines that condemned the accused: the Memphis Appeal used "A Dastardly Outrage" over the deck "Four Negroes Assault a White Woman and Her Little Daughter," and the Wheeling Sunday Register used "Colored Fiends." The dispatch called the alleged crime "the most horrible outrage ever heard of in Tennessee," referred to the men as "brutes" and "scoundrels," and reported the coming lynching as expected news. The Wheeling Register reprinted the story on May 21; the Atlanta Constitution's plainer account made the lynching conditional on the men's guilt.

News of the lynching itself reached readers mostly as one-line items in national digests far from Tennessee. The Los Angeles Daily Herald headed it "Quadruple Lynching"; the Olneyville Times (Rhode Island), the Walker Lake Bulletin (Nevada) and two Michigan weeklies, the True Northerner and the Crawford Avalanche, carried it among news briefs. The Walker Lake Bulletin's item said the men were lynched "for assisting a white woman," evidently a misprint for "assaulting."

The accounts differed on the woman's name: the Chattanooga dispatch called her Mrs. Rice, the Spring City special and the Olneyville Times called her Mrs. Jane Whitney, and the Atlanta Constitution said her name could not be learned. They also differed on how many men were captured (four or three) and on where the lynching took place, near Worthington or from the jail at Washington.

reader.title: Rhea County quadruple lynching
bases: Spring City specials reported that four Black prisoners accused of assaulting a white woman were taken from jail by a mob and lynched (A2, A8, A6).

Two Spring City specials reported the four accused men lynched by a mob that took them from jail for an alleged assault on a white woman (A2, A8, A6), but both are hearsay ('it is reported', 'word has just reached'), no later or local report confirms the deaths, and the Atlanta Constitution on May 22 still described the lynching as a prospect (A5).

The alleged assault and arrests are reported by two separate Chattanooga accounts (A1, A5), but every report of the lynching itself traces to second-hand specials from Spring City (A2, A8), which the digest items repeat (A6, A7).

framing.detail: The Chattanooga wire ran under 'A Dastardly Outrage' and 'Colored Fiends,' called the crime 'the most horrible outrage ever heard of in Tennessee' and the accused 'brutes,' and reported the planned lynching as expected news.
The Atlanta Constitution gave a plain account and conditioned the predicted lynching on the men proving guilty.
Distant papers carried the lynching as one-line digest items or a short special without comment.
